identification.summary: Earth Krahang is the Trend Micro name for a China-linked intrusion set that Trend Micro reported in March 2024 as having been active since early 2022 and focused mainly on government organizations worldwide [S1][S2]. Trend Micro counted at least 70 compromised organizations in 23 countries, 48 of them government bodies, and 116 targeted organizations in 35 countries; other coverage cites 45 countries, so counts vary by source [S3][S4]. The group exploits public-facing servers, sends spear-phishing emails, builds VPN servers on compromised hosts, brute-forces email credentials, and uses access to one government to attack other governments [S1][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Early 2022 per Trend Micro reporting published 2024-03-18 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Trend Micro links Earth Krahang to Earth Lusca but treats it as a separate intrusion set because it has independent infrastructure and unique backdoors [S1][S2]. CYFIRMA, by contrast, lists Earth Krahang as an alias of Earth Lusca, so cluster boundaries differ by vendor [S2]. Trend Micro also raised a possible link to i-Soon, framed as a possibility and not a confirmed attribution [S3][S4]. No Microsoft actor name or MITRE group ID is cited here.

attribution.sponsor: Trend Micro describes the group as China-linked; no government attribution is cited in the gathered sources [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Trend Micro states the Earth Lusca and i-Soon connections as assessments with caveats: Earth Krahang could be another penetration team under the same company as i-Soon, but this is a possibility and not a confirmed attribution [S3][S4]. Vendors disagree on whether Earth Krahang is distinct from Earth Lusca [S1][S2].
attribution.basis: Trend Micro recovered samples, configuration files and attack-tool logs from the group's servers after operational mistakes, and observed shared infrastructure and tactics with Earth Lusca [S1][S2][S5].

objectives: Cyberespionage against government institutions, with stolen email credentials used to exfiltrate mail [S1][S5].

targeting.notes: Trend Micro counted 70 confirmed compromises in 23 countries (48 government) and 116 targets in 35 countries; Security Affairs cites 45 countries [S3][S4]. Lures referenced geopolitical topics such as a Malaysian Ministry of Defense circular, ICJ hearings on Guyana versus Venezuela, and a Malaysian defense minister visit to Hungary [S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via spear-phishing (RAR archives containing LNK files that install backdoors) and exploitation of public-facing servers, including Oracle Web Applications Desktop Integrator CVE-2022-21587 and Openfire CVE-2023-32315; backdoors are sometimes delivered through web shells [S2][S3]. Tooling named in coverage: Cobalt Strike, RESHELL (a simpler .NET backdoor), and XDealer (tracked as DinodasRAT by ESET, with Windows and Linux versions), plus PlugX and ShadowPad listed in HivePro's summary [S2][S3][S7]. Post-exploitation includes SoftEther VPN for persistence and access to internal networks, remote desktop enablement, credential dumping, network scanning, brute-forcing of email accounts, and a Python script to exfiltrate Zimbra mail [S1][S2]. Compromised government webservers and mail accounts host payloads, proxy traffic and send phishing to other governments [S1][S5].

campaigns.name: Earliest observed activity
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro says it has tracked the activity since early 2022.

campaigns.name: Trend Micro public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro published on 2024-03-18 its report describing about 70 compromised organizations in 23 countries, 48 of them government, with a Southeast Asia focus, and its possible links to Earth Lusca and i-Soon.

diamond.adversary: China-linked intrusion set that Trend Micro treats as separate from but related to Earth Lusca, with a possible i-Soon connection [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with RAR/LNK droppers, public-facing server exploits, RESHELL, XDealer/DinodasRAT, Cobalt Strike, SoftEther VPN, and email brute-forcing [S2][S3][S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised government webservers and mail accounts used to host payloads, proxy traffic and send phishing; VPN servers created on compromised hosts; actor-run servers whose logs Trend Micro recovered [S1][S5].
diamond.victim: Government organizations (48 confirmed compromised of about 70), mostly in Southeast Asia [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against governments, using geopolitical lures tied to regional defense and international legal events [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing servers (Oracle, Openfire, Zimbra), Windows and Linux hosts, and email systems with weak credentials [S2][S7].

gaps: Trend Micro's primary report (trendmicro.com) could not be fetched in this session; details rest on search-result summaries and secondary coverage and should be verified against it.
Counts conflict across sources (23 versus 35 versus 45 countries); the basis for each figure was not verified.
Cluster boundary with Earth Lusca (and other vendor names for it) is unresolved; vendors disagree on whether it is a distinct group.
The i-Soon link is explicitly a possibility; no confirmed attribution or government statement was found.
No Earth Krahang activity after March 2024 was found in searches; current status is unknown.
PlugX and ShadowPad use appears only in secondary summaries and was not confirmed in the primary report.
No MITRE group ID or Microsoft name was identified.
Sectors beyond government (telecoms, post offices, media) and the IMDA advisory were not verified and were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Government mail servers, public-facing web and collaboration servers, and inter-government trust relationships are key terrain, since the actor abuses one government's infrastructure to reach others [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The actor favors Southeast Asia but has reached the Americas, Europe and Africa, so coalition and partner governments are in the threat area [S3]. STEP 3: The template is spear-phishing or exploitation of an edge server, then web shell or RESHELL/XDealer, then SoftEther VPN, credential dumping and mail collection [S2][S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued government mail and document collection, including phishing of partner governments from compromised accounts. MDCOA is use of a compromised partner or coalition government account to deliver a backdoor to US or allied defense personnel under a geopolitical lure. Candidate indicators: RAR archives with LNK files from known government senders, new SoftEther VPN services on servers, unexpected web shells on Openfire or Oracle systems, repeated failed email logins, and Linux hosts running unfamiliar systemd/SysV persistence [S2][S1][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track exploitation of edge-server CVEs (CVE-2022-21587, CVE-2023-32315) and partner-government compromises that could cascade to US-bound email [S2]. (2) Authorities: coordinate any defensive action on partner or contractor systems through the proper owners and legal channels; this analysis assigns none. (3) Mission assurance: treat inbound mail from partner governments as potentially compromised and enforce attachment filtering and multi-factor authentication to blunt email brute-forcing [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs, especially in Southeast Asia, and with DC3 and DIB contacts for contractor-hosted servers.

provenance.importedSummary: Earth Krahang is an APT group targeting government organizations worldwide. They use spear-phishing emails, weak internet-facing servers, and custom backdoors like Cobalt Strike, RESHELL, and XDealer to conduct cyber espionage. The group creates VPN servers on infected systems, employs brute force attacks on email accounts, and exploits compromised government infrastructure to attack other governments. Earth Krahang has been linked to another China-linked actor, Earth Lusca, and is believed to be part of a specialized task force for cyber espionage against government institutions.
